    Yes, absolutely =E2=80=94 the reader is plain HTML/CSS/JS w= ith zero dependencies, so you can ship it today. I've packaged it as a stan= dalone page you can host anywhere:
    How to go from here to a product:
      =
    1. Share it as a website fir= st. Drop the file on Netlify, Vercel, or GitHub Pages (all free) a= nd you get a shareable link in minutes. Add a manifest file and it becomes = an installable PWA.
    2. App stores later. Wrap the same code with Capacitor to get iO= S/Android apps from one codebase.
    For subscriptions, you'll need to add:
  • Payments: Stripe for the web; Apple/Google in-app purchase for iOS/Android (t= heir rules require it for digital content =E2=80=94 they take ~15=E2=80=933= 0%)
  • A backend (Supabase or Firebase is enough to start) for accounts, subscriptio= ns, and saving progress/vocabulary across devices
  • Privacy policy + GDPR compliance if you take EU users' data
    • Two honest warnings before you invest:
    • The TTS is th= e weak point. Browser voices are free but inconsistent =E2=80=94 a= n Android user may hear a robotic voice where an Edge user hears a good one= . Paid products usually use a TTS API (Azure, Google, or ElevenLabs =E2=80= =94 check Greek support and per-character costs) or pre-recorded audio.
    • Copyright. "Based on Home Alone" with Kevin, Harry and Marv is fine for a classroom = demo, but risky in a paid product =E2=80=94 film titles, character names an= d story elements are protected. Original stories in the same graded style a= re the safe route. Competitors like LingQ and Readle exist, so the moat is = your content library, not the tap-to-translate tech itself.
    =
    The tech you have is a solid MVP. The= real product is 50=E2=80=93100 well-graded stories with clean audio.
